title: MDPs, value functions, and Bellman equations
summary: Build the RL vocabulary from Markov decision processes to state/action values and optimality backups.

sections.title: Lecture core · MDP vocabulary
sections.body: An MDP describes states, actions, transition and reward dynamics, and a policy. The Markov property says the current state contains the information needed for predicting the next step; the full history need not be carried forward.

math.explanation: The return is the discounted sum of future rewards from time $t$. The exponent starts at zero for the next reward, so the immediate reward is not discounted; later rewards receive progressively smaller weights when $0legamma<1$.

sections.title: Textbook depth · Value functions
sections.body: A state value is the expected return from a state under a policy. An action value conditions on both the state and the first action. The Bellman equation turns a long-horizon return into a local reward plus a discounted continuation value.

math.explanation: The value function averages the return over trajectories generated by policy $\pi$. The Bellman form exposes the recursion: immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state.

symbols.meaning: expected return from state $s$ under policy $\pi$
probability of choosing action $a$ in state $s$

sections.title: Textbook depth · Policy versus optimality
sections.body: The policy Bellman equation averages over actions using $\pi(a\mid s)$. The optimality equation replaces that average with a maximum. This is the conceptual jump behind value iteration and Q-learning.

math.explanation: The optimal value asks which first action gives the highest expected continuation. The transition model still averages over possible next states and rewards; only the policy choice changes from a fixed average to a maximizing decision.

sections.title: Reference boundary
sections.body: The RL reference is optional background for algorithm comparisons. Secure the MDP, return, value, and Bellman core before adding algorithm names to your revision notes.

examples.title: Worked example: discount a delayed reward
steps: A trajectory gives reward 1 now and reward 10 two steps later.
With $\gamma=0.9$, it is $1+0.9^2\times10=9.1$. The larger discount makes delayed reward matter much more.
examples.answer: Changing $\gamma$ changes the objective: it is not merely a learning-rate setting.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What changes in behavior as $\gamma$ approaches zero?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare the immediate-reward term with the discounted continuation terms.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The agent becomes nearly myopic: immediate reward dominates and delayed consequences contribute little.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does the Markov property matter for tractable value functions?
criticalQuestions.angle: Ask whether the same state can imply different futures because of hidden history.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: If the state summarizes all decision-relevant history, one value function can condition on the state. If not, the process appears non-Markov and the value estimate can mix incompatible situations.
